[{"id":5312629055,"body":"### 2026-08-17 — promote run

Targets (local packs changed in the window, per dispatch #870's Context): ClaudiniteWebsite, EdFringeNow, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, LaughCounter, MissingBulbWebsite, Sheepdog, TLDR, VascularColoring.

**Promoted — 20 lessons, all prose rung (judgment / runtime behavior / signature-less tool-usage knowledge — none had a reliable static signature a check could carry) → PR [#949](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/949) (branch `growth-promote-8r1x`):**

| origin | landed | generalized rule |
|---|---|---|
| ClaudiniteWebsite + Sheepdog | `git-github-advanced/SKILL.md` | A local git-mutation refusal after a merge already succeeded server-side isn't worth a second retry variant — take one attempt, state local is behind, verify read-only instead. |
| EdFringeNow | `git-github-advanced/SKILL.md` | A shallow checkout breaks `git merge-base` (false "orphaned"/"unrelated" verdicts); unshallow before trusting a cross-branch history comparison. |
| MissingBulbWebsite | `git-github-advanced/SKILL.md` | Prefer `git commit && git push` over the MCP file-write tools for a file already correct on disk — they transcribe the file, not copy it. |
| EdFringeNow | `git-github-advanced/SKILL.md` | A run stuck `queued` (auto-cancels ~15min) or dying in an early platform setup step is infrastructure, not a CI failure to wait out or diagnose. |
| EdFringeNow | `git-github-advanced/SKILL.md` (fold) | `get_job_logs` needs `failed_only:true` or a fetched `job_id`, and 404s on an in-progress job. |
| GoogleCalendarEventCreator + Sheepdog | `core/scheduled-tasks.md` | Claiming a dispatch swaps its label, which re-fires the webhook that started you — a duplicate trigger for an issue you already hold is usually your own echo, not a new signal. |
| Sheepdog | `core/RULES.md` | A canon skill's relative links resolve against its real mounted path, not the `Skill` tool's announced per-session flat base directory. |
| Sheepdog | `basics/RULES.md` | `Grep`'s context flags (`-n`/`-A`/`-B`/`-C`) are silently ignored without `output_mode: "content"`. |
| MissingBulbWebsite | `basics/RULES.md` | Never publish a claim about a real named person on a substituted weaker source or a "please verify" caveat — verify or ask the person, or leave it out. |
| MissingBulbWebsite | `basics/RULES.md` (fold) | An egress block is domain-wide and distinct from a per-site `403` — don't work down alternate sources, and don't file an unresolvable "re-verify next pass". |
| EdFringeNow | `basics/RULES.md` (fold) | Litmus test for a cross-file dependency comment: if the detail wouldn't force the dependent file to change, it's the dependency's detail, not the dependent's. |
| TLDR | `basics/RULES.md` | Piping a long command through `tail`/`head` discards its real exit code and truncates earlier summary lines — redirect to a file and read `$?` from that invocation. |
| LaughCounter | `basics/RULES.md` (fold) | A repo-scanning check must strip comments in **both** directions (a warning comment about the banned pattern, and a commented-out instance) and be proven silent against the repo's real sources, not only a synthetic fixture. |
| EdFringeNow | `extracting-lessons.md` | Never capture a rule that teaches routing around a permission/security/classifier denial, however solid the retry evidence — report a recurring denial to the owner instead. |
| LaughCounter + Sheepdog | `unattended-agents/SKILL.md` | A `[Merge Without Review]` warning on a task's own licensed unattended merge is expected — adjudicate against the declared delivery policy/ceiling in one step, don't escalate every occurrence. |
| Sheepdog + ClaudiniteWebsite | `unattended-agents/SKILL.md` | A background subagent shares the parent's working directory unless isolated — its uncommitted WIP or a branch switch can look like the parent's own state to an end-of-session check. |
| Sheepdog | `writing-tests/SKILL.md` | Restore a see-it-fail mutation with `git checkout`/`stash` taken at the moment of mutating, never an earlier `.bak`. |
| Sheepdog | `writing-tests/SKILL.md` | A retry/requeue/hand-off helper needs a test that calls it twice; when the mechanism arbitrates by identity, the second call must come from a different actor. |
| Sheepdog | `writing-tests/SKILL.md` | A stateful simulator must model what the real engine's code writes, never the rule's stated intent. |
| Sheepdog | `bug-investigation/SKILL.md` | A bug theory predicts what you'll find; quote a regenerated run's own log for what it actually did rather than reasoning forward from the diagnosis. |
| EdFringeNow | `headless-browser/RULES.md` (fold) | Reinstalling a browser-driver package to fix an import error can pull a version mismatched with the environment's pinned browser. |

No stub pack minted — every lesson had an existing canon owner.

**Notable rejections (dedup verified against the current corpus, not memory):**
- The `search_issues`/`fields`/`per_page` MCP-token-limit cluster (ClaudiniteWebsite, MissingBulbWebsite, Sheepdog, GoogleCalendarEventCreator) — already fully covered by `git-github-advanced`'s "Cap and qualify every list/search call" section, including the semantic-matching-vs-`in:title` gotcha and the fields-not-just-page-size point.
- `ScheduleWakeup` requiring `prompt` (ClaudiniteWebsite) — already in `basics/RULES.md`.
- A long tail of git/GitHub, Playwright/headless-browser, HTML-parsing, prose-to-checks-meta and research-methodology items from EdFringeNow, GoogleCalendarEventCreator, LaughCounter, MissingBulbWebsite and VascularColoring matched existing canon rules verbatim or near-verbatim — those repos were confirmed as earlier promotion sources (EdFringeNow → `headless-browser`, LaughCounter → `prose-to-checks`, VascularColoring → `research-project`, GoogleCalendarEventCreator/MissingBulbWebsite → `git-github-advanced`/`unattended-agents`).
- All product-specific content (extractor pipelines, audio-hardware lifecycle, on-device-privacy policy, site copy, data-pipeline calibration) stayed in its origin repo, as required.

One process note from this run: a `git checkout -b <branch> main` against a **stale local `main`** (34 commits behind `origin/main`) silently based the work on old canon content mid-run — caught only because a dedup result looked implausibly different from an earlier read of the same file. Recovered by resetting to `origin/main` before any commit landed; no lesson promoted from it this round since it's this task's own procedural footgun, not a portable one — worth a `growth-promote` task-doc note in a future pass if it recurs.

| EdFringeNow | `basics/RULES.md` (fold) | Litmus test for a cross-file dependency comment: if the detail wouldn't force the dependent file to change, it's the dependency's detail, not the dependent's. |

The claudinite-website pack's prose warned that a bare `node --test` skips
this repo's dot-directories, finds zero tests and exits green. That is a
static signature — the invocations live in package.json scripts and workflow
run: steps — so it becomes a check instead: an invocation's arguments must
resolve to at least one path that exists in the tree.

The check asserts the stronger property the prose asked a human to confirm by
eye (a non-zero test count), so it also catches a glob that has gone stale.
The prose paragraph is deleted whole: its what/why/fix now live in the
finding and the module's header comment.

CI gains the step that runs the pack fixtures — with the explicit glob the
new rule requires, so the fixture is not itself silently green.

Final hindsight pass over the 17 conversation logs past the 10-day
retention window (all captured 2026-08-07), plus a fresh pass over the
2026-08-16/17 logs. Six new lessons landed in edfringe/RULES.md:

- amend the latest commit (not git filter-branch) once the
  task-lifecycle Stop hook has already fired
- never curl api.github.com directly for a run's status — it returns a
  look-alike JSON error with no status field, so a naive poll loop
  spins silently forever; poll through the GitHub MCP tools
- pull_request_read method=get_status is a dead signal on this repo —
  use get_check_runs
- a deleted workflow file's old runs can't be purged by any session
  tool (no actions:write DELETE endpoint in the MCP toolset) — hand it
  to the owner
- npm i -D playwright in the repo root is the same footgun as the
  scratchpad variant, just quieter
- index.html's Leaflet map loads from unpkg.com, which the sandbox
  proxy blocks — stub it before driving the page

None of the six clear the check-the-world test (all are session/API
runtime behavior, not static repo signatures), so all land as prose.

Conversation half — 5 lessons added to .claudinite/local/packs/edfringe/RULES.md:

- A Bash `wait` call in its own invocation waits for nothing (fresh shell,
  no earlier child to wait on) — extends the existing blind-sleep section,
  from #368.
- A GitHub Actions run that executed none of the repo's own steps is
  infrastructure, not a CI failure to wait out — recognise it and stop
  recommending "keep waiting", from #239/#237.
- GitHub MCP call shapes that cost round-trips here: `actions_list` token
  overflow isn't fixed by lowering `per_page`, `list_pull_requests` never
  reports `merged: true`, and `get_job_logs` needs `failed_only`/a job id —
  from #372 and #237.
- The sandbox checkout is shallow, which fails `git merge-base` for older
  branches and reads as false "orphaned" in tidy-branches — from #375.
- A stuck `[claudinite-task]` issue's bot-comment pile is the stale-dispatch
  watchdog, not proof the job is recurring-failing — verify against the
  actual run log before shipping a fix — from #237.

#382/#380/#387) is upstream Claudinite queue-wiring config and routine
automated reports, already assessed by the prior run for a8fa814/#383/#382/#380;

The refresh-tickets task ran hourly through August, so a festival day put
up to sixteen "Refresh ticket status" commits into main and expired every
browser's copy of the day file as many times — for a status that is a
snapshot however often it is taken. The churn was judged not worth the
freshness.

The cadence becomes `daily+1h` (05:00 UTC, 06:00 Edinburgh): a slot clear
of the `daily` anchor refresh-shows holds, so availability is refreshed
after the catalogue top-up that may have added the shows it is about, and
the repo's two data-committing tasks never share a checkout.

The precondition's 08:00–23:59 hours window goes with the hourly cadence.
A once-a-day task has one evaluation to spend and that window would have
rejected the 06:00 one every day — leaving the task declared, evaluated,
and silently never running. The August gate stays, since that is the part
that was ever about the data. window.test.mjs now pins the failure the
removal guards against: no hour of an August day may gate the slot out.

Everything that documented the hourly cadence is updated with it — the
scraper README's task table and cache-TTL table, normalize.py and
refresh_ticket_status.py's module docs, the edfringe-data rules, and the
client cache comments. The now page keeps its one-hour day-file TTL
deliberately, no longer to match the refresh but so a hand-run refresh
reaches an open tab the same day; the README and js/app.js say so.

Closes #341

The Claudinite scheduler runs every due task in ONE checkout, and
basics/baselining's deliver() does `git checkout -B <maintenance branch>`
and never switches back. A task ordered after a delivering baselining
therefore inherits a branch with no upstream, and its bare `git push`
aborts with exit 128 — which silently stopped a data refresh twice
(#141 on refresh-shows, #231 on refresh-tickets), each time for days,
each time surfacing only as a needs-human dispatch issue.

Both workers now carry the branch-restore guard, but nothing enforced it:
the next worker.sh added to a local pack would omit it and fail the same
way a third time. edfringe-worker-restores-main makes that omission a
blocking finding — every .claudinite/local/packs/*/tasks/*/worker.sh that
commits or pushes must return the checkout to `main` first, and must do
it before the write rather than after.

The check's fix line also warns off the workaround that looks obvious and
is wrong: `git push origin HEAD:main` succeeds from a polluted checkout,
which is exactly how baselining's unreviewed converge would reach main
past its own maintenance PR.

Seen to fail on a violating fixture, on a restore placed after the write,
and against the real tree with the guard removed from refresh-shows;
green on the tree as it stands. Full offline suite green (274 tests).

The conversation half found nothing new: the friction in the aging logs
(issue-first, comment-classification, visual verification, work-procedure
-vs-product-requirement) is already captured in the pack's RULES.md, and
the availability-cache lesson from the 2026-08-09 sessions has already
landed in the static-website canon. 16 logs past the 10-day retention got
their final hindsight pass and were pruned from conversation-logs.

The Claudinite scheduler runs every due task in ONE checkout, and
basics/baselining's deliver() does `git checkout -B <maintenance branch>`
and never switches back. A task ordered after a delivering baselining
therefore inherits a branch with no upstream, and its bare `git push`
aborts with exit 128 — which silently stopped a data refresh twice
(#141 on refresh-shows, #231 on refresh-tickets), each time for days,
each time surfacing only as a needs-human dispatch issue.

Both workers now carry the branch-restore guard, but nothing enforced it:
the next worker.sh added to a local pack would omit it and fail the same
way a third time. edfringe-worker-restores-main makes that omission a
blocking finding — every .claudinite/local/packs/*/tasks/*/worker.sh that
commits or pushes must return the checkout to `main` first, and must do
it before the write rather than after.

The check's fix line also warns off the workaround that looks obvious and
is wrong: `git push origin HEAD:main` succeeds from a polluted checkout,
which is exactly how baselining's unreviewed converge would reach main
past its own maintenance PR.

Seen to fail on a violating fixture, on a restore placed after the write,
and against the real tree with the guard removed from refresh-shows;
green on the tree as it stands. Full offline suite green (274 tests).

The conversation half found nothing new: the friction in the aging logs
(issue-first, comment-classification, visual verification, work-procedure
-vs-product-requirement) is already captured in the pack's RULES.md, and
the availability-cache lesson from the 2026-08-09 sessions has already
landed in the static-website canon. 16 logs past the 10-day retention got
their final hindsight pass and were pruned from conversation-logs.

Conversation-extract run over the logs captured 2026-07-30/31. The
merge-and-ci skill's post-merge section claims the checkout is "the one
part that stalls or gets denied" and that the bare `git fetch origin
main` "succeeded on the first try". Newer captures contradict that:

- session `ee3cdc13` (2026-07-30): bare `git fetch origin main` denied
  by the auto-mode classifier at 22:43:35→22:44:11 (36s), and the
  identical immediate retry denied again at 22:44:17→22:45:04 (47s).
  The session gave up and ran capture-log.mjs anyway — which worked.
- session `19e34589` (2026-07-31): denied at 05:13:46→05:14:21 (35s);
  the identical retry then passed in 9s.

So the denial is non-deterministic and not scoped to the checkout. The
rule that follows: budget exactly one retry at ~30-45s a denial, then
proceed — nothing downstream needs the fetch, and a denial here is never
an error to report, escalate, or work around by decomposing the command.

Adds the measured paragraph to the skill's post-merge section, softens
the now-wrong "the one part" claim, and adds the row to the pack
README's rules table.

* create-extractor: hand the agent its draft PR by identity, not by branch prefix

The agent was told to find its draft PR by the `claude/extractor/` head-branch
prefix. A search that finds nothing is indistinguishable from nothing having been
created, and the agent believes it — the failure mode Claudinite #649 records,
where a delivered-and-merged PR read as "this cycle delivered nothing".

Preprocessing already knows both values at the moment it hands off, so it now
writes them into the agent-request file; the scheduler renders them into the
dispatch issue as `### Delivered by preprocessing`, and §1 reads them there. No
section means preprocessing created nothing, and that is authoritative — there is
no fallback search, because the fallback is the bug.

The `claude/extractor/` prefix survives only as this task's own bookkeeping for
reclaiming stale requests; it is nobody's lookup key now. Everything else the
agent needs — the scaffold, the recorded page — still comes from reading the
repo, per agent-preprocessing DESIGN §3, whose narrow exception for artifact
identity this uses.

DO NOT MERGE until the engine change (missingbulb/Claudinite#657) has reached
this repo's mount: until then nothing writes the section §1 now reads, and the
agent would take its absence at face value.

* create-extractor: hand the agent its draft PR by identity, not by branch prefix

The agent was told to find its draft PR by the `claude/extractor/` head-branch
prefix. A search that finds nothing is indistinguishable from nothing having been
created, and the agent believes it — the failure mode Claudinite #649 records,
where a delivered-and-merged PR read as "this cycle delivered nothing".

Preprocessing already knows both values at the moment it hands off, so it now
writes them into the agent-request file; the scheduler renders them into the
dispatch issue as `### Delivered by preprocessing`, and §1 reads them there. No
section means preprocessing created nothing, and that is authoritative — there is
no fallback search, because the fallback is the bug.

The `claude/extractor/` prefix survives only as this task's own bookkeeping for
reclaiming stale requests; it is nobody's lookup key now. Everything else the
agent needs — the scaffold, the recorded page — still comes from reading the
repo, per agent-preprocessing DESIGN §3, whose narrow exception for artifact
identity this uses.

DO NOT MERGE until the engine change (missingbulb/Claudinite#657) has reached
this repo's mount: until then nothing writes the section §1 now reads, and the
agent would take its absence at face value.

* Claudinite growth: discover local pack macos-audio-lifecycle

The macOS microphone lifecycle is a technology domain this repo carries real,
hard-won knowledge for (dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md, 505 lines of case
history across #22/#61/#72/#76/#79/#88/#107), that no canon pack homes and that
neither existing local pack owns — on-device-privacy owns the privacy boundary,
laughcounter the repo's build/packaging and check-authoring lessons.

Nothing enforced any of it. This lands the invariants as a pack with three
checks, each red on a fixture and green on the repo's real files:

- engine-construction-confined — only AudioHub builds an AVAudioEngine, because
  constructing one opens the default input and churns a hidden coreaudiod
  aggregate device; AudioDiagnostics answers availability from HAL property
  queries that open nothing.
- signal-teardown-routing — a tree that installs an audio tap must route
  SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP to NSApp.terminate, with SIG_IGN before resume().
- no-sudden-termination — Info.plist must never opt into sudden termination,
  which would let logout SIGKILL the app past every teardown path.

The judgment half lands as RULES.md prose (open no device to ask a question,
presence is not usability, a duration is only as good as the observation behind
it, clock choice across sleep, generation-guarded deferred work, never claim
"listening" on engine.start() returning, compile-green is not a gate, assume no
toolchain on the owner's Mac). The case history stays in dev/procedures/ rather
than being copied, so there is one source for it.

Also narrows laughcounter's routing excludes so the new territory routes cleanly.

* Convert the Comment class: menu-restating rule to a check (tldr pack)

The prose-to-checks sweep over .claudinite/local/packs found one rule whose
deterministic half was still only prose: naming the other classes on the
`Comment class:` line declares them, because the classifier reads the whole
line and adds every token `classesIn()` matches.

Adds tldr/comment-class-menu (scope: work, advisory) — it fires when a class
token appears after a negation marker on the classification line and was not
already named before it, which separates restating the menu from an honest
multi-class declaration. Advisory rather than blocking on purpose: the
transcript is append-only, so a blocking finding could never converge.

Fixture proves both directions (blind mutation reds the two firing cases,
dropping the positional guard reds two silent cases).

Deletion test: the remedy paragraph is deleted whole — the finding's fix line
now carries the class-alone remedy, the next-line placement, and the
honest-multi-class exemption. The mechanism paragraph and the append-only
incident record stay: the finding carries neither the worked bad line nor the
2026-07-26 cost evidence.

* Check the mandated Comment class: form, not the author's intent

Refs #159

The first draft of tldr/comment-class-menu inferred intent: it fired only
on a class token appearing after a negation word from a hand-picked list
("not", "never", "besides", ...). The harm, though, comes from a class
token being present at all — classesIn() matches globally and negates
nothing — so prose smuggles classes in without tripping any marker.

Probed against the real helper, the old detector stayed silent on:

  Comment class: other — unrelated to any feature request       declares feature
  Comment class: other, setting the feature question to one side declares feature
  Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other   declares all four

The last is the menu pasted verbatim out of the classifier's own prompt —
the likeliest way this bug is reproduced, missed by the check named for it.

RULES.md mandates a verbatim form (the class alone, explanation on the next
line), so assert that instead: the declaration must be class tokens joined
by a declaration separator and nothing else. `|` is deliberately not a
separator, so a menu paste fails rather than reading as a four-class
declaration. No word list, and a conforming line has nowhere to hide a
token. An honest multi-class declaration stays silent.

Fixture grows to 11 cases, mutation-proven in both directions: blinding the
pattern reddens the 5 firing cases, allowing `|` reddens the menu-paste
case, and dropping the end-anchor reddens all 5.

1	# Headless browser
2	
3	Driving a real browser from your own process — a page loaded, faked, driven and captured by code
4	rather than by a user. True whether the output is a golden image, a build artifact, or an
5	assertion about behaviour, and whether the driver is Playwright or Puppeteer.
6	
7	Two neighbours own ground this pack deliberately does not restate: **which** engine a UI golden
8	should be rendered with, what tolerance it may carry, and the approval gate before re-baselining
9	one belong to the [writing-tests](../basics/skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md) skill; wiring the run
10	into a workflow belongs to [github-actions](../github-actions/). This pack is the browser itself.
11	
12	## Getting a browser
13	
14	- **Resolve the binary out of the environment; never let the driver download one.** A container
15	  or runner image that already ships a browser is the normal case, and the driver's own registry
16	  download is slow, often blocked, and pins a build you did not choose. Look for an explicit
17	  override variable first, then the image's browser root, then fall through to the driver's own
18	  resolution — and prefer the driver's `-core` package, which bundles no browser at all. The
19	  image's build number need not match the driver's own pin for the browser to launch. Never
20	  hardcode the version-stamped path you found by looking: it moves with the next image, and the
21	  failure lands on whoever rebuilds rather than on whoever wrote it.
22	
23	- **A fresh install of the driver package is the same danger from upstream.** Reinstalling the
24	  package to fix an import error just as easily resolves to a newer release than the one paired
25	  with the environment's pinned browser — it then hunts for a browser build the image was never
26	  given and fails asking for a network install the sandbox cannot make. Resolve the
27	  already-installed package by its global path instead of adding a second copy.
28	
29	- **A committed pixel golden is only comparable under the exact build that rendered it.** Two
30	  browsers a version apart rasterise text and shadows differently, so a comparison across them
31	  measures the renderer, not the product. Where the output is compared pixel by pixel, read the
32	  installed driver version at launch and **refuse to run** on any other, naming the pinned one in
33	  the error; where it is not — a build artifact, a behavioural assertion — let the build float
34	  and spend nothing on pinning it.
35	
36	- **Pinning is what buys a zero-diff browser golden — budget for the whole recipe or accept a
37	  tolerance.** A browser screenshot is not bit-stable across machines by default, which is why
38	  the general advice is a small tolerance. It *can* be made bit-stable, and the price is this
39	  pack's next two sections in full: the pinned build, a font jail, and the rasterisation flags.
40	  Take all of it or take the tolerance; a half-applied recipe gives a zero-diff gate that fails
41	  on someone else's machine for reasons no one can read off the diff.
42	
43	## The page's world is an input — replace all of it
44	
45	- **Serve the page from a fake origin you fulfil from disk, and abort anything you did not
46	  name.** Intercepting at the browser needs no server process, no port and no free-port race,
47	  and it reaches *every* request the page makes rather than the ones an application-level mock
48	  happens to know about. Make the default arm an abort: a new external dependency then breaks
49	  the run loudly instead of quietly adding real network to a run meant to be hermetic.
50	
51	- **Use an `https` fake origin.** Geolocation and several other capabilities exist only on a
52	  secure origin, and a page served over `http` silently takes the denied path instead. Routes
53	  are fulfilled before any connection is attempted, so no certificate is involved and nothing
54	  has to be trusted.
55	
56	- **Route a vendored third-party asset host-agnostically.** A stylesheet you serve in place of a
57	  CDN copy still resolves *its own* relative URLs against the host it was served from, so the
58	  font or image files it references arrive addressed to that CDN. Match those follow-up requests
59	  on the path alone, on any host, or the sheet loads and every asset it names 404s — which
60	  renders as a silent fallback rather than an error.
61	
62	- **Know which knobs are fixed at context creation and which are per page.** Locale, timezone,
63	  viewport, device scale factor, geolocation and permissions belong to the browser *context* and
64	  cannot be changed once it exists — so proving that a product reads a fixed zone rather than
65	  the device's takes **two** contexts, not one page reconfigured twice. The clock, seeded
66	  randomness and injected scripts are per page.
67	
68	- **A command-line window-size flag is not a viewport — a narrow one does not test the narrow
69	  layout.** Ask a browser's *CLI* for a phone-sized window and it renders the page at a clamped
70	  width and crops the overflow, without applying the media queries the width should have
71	  triggered. The output looks exactly like a horizontal-overflow bug in every section of a page
72	  that has none, and the instinct is to go hunting through the CSS for the offender. Only a
73	  context or page created with an explicit viewport puts the page in that layout. Reserve the
74	  CLI screenshot for the width the window happens to be, and give it a virtual-time budget that
75	  outlasts the page's entrance animations, or sections capture mid-transition and read as broken
76	  when they are fine.
77	
78	- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
79	  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
80	  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.
81	
82	- **Freezing CSS animation does not freeze the Web Animations API.** Zeroing
83	  `animation-duration` and `transition-duration` stops declarative animation and nothing else;
84	  anything driven through `element.animate` keeps running, and a capture races it. Stub the
85	  method so every such animation resolves on its end state immediately.
86	
87	- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
88	  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
89	  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
90	  has no timers to advance.
91	
92	## Fonts decide the layout, and the machine decides the fonts
93	
94	- **Vendoring the web fonts is half the job — every glyph they lack is drawn from the machine.**
95	  An emoji, an arrow, a currency sign, a non-Latin title: each falls back to whatever the host
96	  has installed, so the rendering quietly becomes a record of that machine's font set. The
97	  failure is brutal and unobvious — one string measures wider on a runner than on a workstation,
98	  wraps, and every card below it moves down a line. Launch the browser with its own
99	  font-configuration world whose only font directory is one you vendored, with the generic
100	  families aliased into it, so nothing installed on the host can reach the page.
101	
102	- **Ask the browser for reproducible rasterisation.** Disable hinting and subpixel text, force
103	  an sRGB colour profile, hide scrollbars, and disable GPU rasterisation. Shadows and blurs need
104	  two more: partial raster reuses tiles whose seams land inside a blur, and runtime-optimised
105	  drawing routines differ by CPU — both make the *same* page render differently run to run on
106	  one machine.
107	
108	## Capturing
109	
110	- **Wait on something the page itself produces, never on the network going quiet.** A selector
111	  that only exists once data rendered, or text that only appears once an async read returned, is
112	  a real signal; "no requests for a moment" is a guess that is wrong in both directions. Await
113	  font readiness too — text laid out before the fonts land is a different image.
114	
115	- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
116	  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
117	  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
118	  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
119	  deliberately before measuring anything.
120	
121	- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
122	  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
123	  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
124	  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.
125	
126	- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
127	  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
128	  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
129	  is an error, not a crop.
130	
131	- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
132	  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
133	  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
134	  meant to show yourself.
135	
136	- **Launch once and reuse the browser across captures.** Process startup dominates the cost of a
137	  capture, so a fresh browser per shot turns a fast run into a slow one for nothing; take a new
138	  context or page per capture instead, and close it, so no state leaks between them.

  triggered. The output looks exactly like a horizontal-overflow bug in every section of a page
  that has none, and the instinct is to go hunting through the CSS for the offender. Only a
  context or page created with an explicit viewport puts the page in that layout. Reserve the
  CLI screenshot for the width the window happens to be, and give it a virtual-time budget that
  outlasts the page's entrance animations, or sections capture mid-transition and read as broken
  when they are fine.

- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.

- **Freezing CSS animation does not freeze the Web Animations API.** Zeroing
  `animation-duration` and `transition-duration` stops declarative animation and nothing else;
  anything driven through `element.animate` keeps running, and a capture races it. Stub the
  method so every such animation resolves on its end state immediately.

- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
  has no timers to advance.

## Fonts decide the layout, and the machine decides the fonts

- **Vendoring the web fonts is half the job — every glyph they lack is drawn from the machine.**
  An emoji, an arrow, a currency sign, a non-Latin title: each falls back to whatever the host
  has installed, so the rendering quietly becomes a record of that machine's font set. The
  failure is brutal and unobvious — one string measures wider on a runner than on a workstation,
  wraps, and every card below it moves down a line. Launch the browser with its own
  font-configuration world whose only font directory is one you vendored, with the generic
  families aliased into it, so nothing installed on the host can reach the page.

- **Ask the browser for reproducible rasterisation.** Disable hinting and subpixel text, force
  an sRGB colour profile, hide scrollbars, and disable GPU rasterisation. Shadows and blurs need
  two more: partial raster reuses tiles whose seams land inside a blur, and runtime-optimised
  drawing routines differ by CPU — both make the *same* page render differently run to run on
  one machine.

## Capturing

- **Wait on something the page itself produces, never on the network going quiet.** A selector
  that only exists once data rendered, or text that only appears once an async read returned, is
  a real signal; "no requests for a moment" is a guess that is wrong in both directions. Await
  font readiness too — text laid out before the fonts land is a different image.

- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
  deliberately before measuring anything.

- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.

- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
  is an error, not a crop.

- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
  meant to show yourself.

- **Launch once and reuse the browser across captures.** Process startup dominates the cost of a
  capture, so a fresh browser per shot turns a fast run into a slow one for nothing; take a new
  context or page per capture instead, and close it, so no state leaks between them.

---
name: unattended-agents
description: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
---

# Agent architecture principles

Portable rules for *how to structure an unattended (automation-invoked) agent* — the judgment-boundary and write-surface guarantees that keep a workflow-driven agent bounded and reliable, independent of any one project.

- An agent invoked **unattended** by automation (a CI workflow, not interactive Claude Code) should be left only the part of the task that genuinely needs its judgment; hard-code every deterministic part — the setup before *and* the wrap-up after — in the workflow around it. A step described in prose is one the agent can skip, reorder, or improvise; a step the workflow runs in code can't be fumbled, and the shorter prompt keeps the agent on the one thing only it can do. Push that boundary continually: each time a step proves mechanical, move it out of the prompt and into the workflow.
- When a routine needs a capability its own runtime lacks — a credential spanning more repos than the session's allowlist, an execution surface the sandbox can't reach — wrap that part as a **dispatch-only executor** (e.g. a `workflow_dispatch`-only GitHub Actions workflow holding the privileged token) that the routine triggers and awaits. The executor carries **no schedule of its own**: give it a cron and it silently becomes a second orchestrator with a competing trigger. One schedule, owned by the orchestrating routine; executors run only when dispatched. State only the executor's *contract* in the routine's prose (what it computes, what the agent may rely on) — its internal rules live in its code, unlike validators of the agent's *own* output, which the prose must still teach (see the routine-folder rules below).
- **The routine's own in-session steps reach GitHub through the session's MCP tools — never a REST client or a `GITHUB_TOKEN`.** This is the corollary of the rule above: the steps a routine runs *itself* operate over the repos the session was granted, which the MCP GitHub tools already cover, so they need no token. A REST client, a raw `api.github.com` `fetch`, or a `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` read in in-session code (a migration pass, an agent-stage worker doc's steps) is the tell that the step was mis-built as if it were the CI *executor* — and it will 401 in the MCP-only session it's scheduled in, silently turning the run into a no-op. Only the part that genuinely needs the broader credential moves to a dispatch-only executor; everything else is MCP. *Diagnosing* whether in-session code can reach a host: probe with a tool that honors the sandbox's `HTTPS_PROXY` — `curl` does — never a bare `node -e "fetch(...)"`, whose global `fetch` ignores `HTTPS_PROXY` and goes **direct**, returning a verdict that bypasses (and so misreports) the proxy's real one.
- Size a routine spec at checklist altitude, and re-compress after every scope addition — specs bloat by accretion, not by any one edit. Keep it to terse imperative bullets stating outcomes, bounds, and judgment criteria; a delegated step gets its contract only, procedure another doc owns gets a pointer (never a restatement), and a why-clause earns its place only where the rule is surprising. Symptoms you've absorbed what belongs elsewhere: the spec re-explains a companion script's logic or a sibling doc's steps, or has grown to several times its sibling routines (the house norm is ~40–90 lines).
- Bound an unattended agent's **write surface**, and enforce it from outside the agent. Pre-create the exact file(s) it may edit, tell it to touch nothing else (no new files, no edits to shared code it might be tempted to "improve"), and after it stops, verify the diff in the workflow — reverting anything outside the allowed set rather than trusting the prompt. Prose is a request; the post-hoc diff check is the guarantee, so a misbehaving agent's blast radius is bounded no matter how it strays. Anything the agent would otherwise reach into belongs inlined in its own file (as a source's local helper), not edited in place.
- In a multi-stage unattended pipeline, converge **every** failure exit — including an infrastructure failure in a pre-agent setup stage (a fetch, an auth step, scaffolding) — to the same human-triage state as an agent-detected failure. A setup-phase failure that reports itself but leaves the original trigger untouched (e.g. a label still set) makes the item look unprocessed rather than blocked, silently defeating the escalation path. Treat every failure mode as equivalent from the triage perspective.
- An unattended agent must **never invoke a tool that surfaces a blocking approval it cannot answer** — there is no human present to click "Allow," so the run stalls indefinitely on step one. The multi-agent-orchestration **Workflow tool is the classic trap**: it mandates an interactive opt-in on *every* run (the prompt only disappears under bypass-permissions / headless modes you cannot rely on the scheduler being in), so a routine that fans out through it hangs before doing any work. Fan out with **plain subagent dispatch** (the Agent/Task tool) instead — it carries no such gate and the orchestrator honors any phase barriers itself — and reserve the Workflow tool for interactive sessions where a human can consent. The general rule: an unattended agent's whole tool path must be answer-free.
- **Dispatch a subagent under worktree isolation whenever it may commit.** Without it the child works in the parent's checkout and leaves it wherever it finished — on the child's branch — so the parent's branch-scoped end-of-session checks judge the *child's* commits against the *parent's* transcript and file findings the parent cannot act on. Pass the isolation flag on the dispatch (`isolation: "worktree"`); recovering after the fact means checking the parent back onto its own assigned branch and re-verifying everything.
- **A routine that correctly declines has not failed — converge failures, not declines.** When the item a run was dispatched for genuinely cannot be processed (an unreachable source, a dead link, an empty result), record the reason on that item, mark it for human attention, and exit **zero**. Failing the task instead raises a *second* human-triage signal for the same item and reports the pipeline as broken when it in fact judged correctly. Partial success is the same shape: the items that did process still land.
- **A run that *skips* its work still exits 0 — a job whose success and whose no-op look identical from outside is telling you nothing.** A scheduler ran green nightly while skipping its main stage on a misread config value, the only trace one skip line in a log nobody opens on a green run. Make every skip state what it skipped and why in the run's own visible output, and confirm a routine works by reading a *reason*, not an exit code: a skip is a finding to triage, not a pass. And when the defect lives inside the mechanism that updates itself (a vendored mount its own maintenance job refreshes, a bootstrap that installs its own successor), the ordinary route can't carry the fix — recognise the self-reference and land the repair out of band rather than waiting for the broken updater.
- **The session that designed a judgment stage must not be the one that runs it.** A stage that picks the strongest candidate, ranks a set, or decides what matters has to run in a context that never saw it being built — the designing session knows which candidates it had in mind when it chose the heuristic and will find them again, which is an echo, not judgment. Exercise a freshly-built stage in a subagent whose context starts empty, or leave it to the scheduler. Better, make the clean context **structural rather than remembered**: state it in the task spec as a rule the agent reads every run ("do not load context you were not given — the item's own title, body and discussion are what you have, and they are enough"), so the production path is clean without anyone arranging it.
- **A rejected call whose whole purpose was a fallback must be re-issued before you continue.** Arming a timeout wake-up, a watchdog, or a retry is the one class of call whose rejection changes nothing observable: the error scrolls past mid-turn, the run proceeds believing it holds a safety net it never armed, and the gap surfaces only when the primary path dies and nothing recovers it. Read the result of every guard-arming call, re-issue it on the spot, and never claim to be relying on a backstop you didn't confirm.
- **Nothing you post to a tracker can be edited — resolve every value before the comment goes up.** The GitHub toolsets these runs use offer comment *creation* and no comment-update tool, so a comment that goes out wrong can only be appended to, leaving the wrong value and its correction both standing forever. An agent session also has **no ambient clock**: a timestamp is only true if you read it (one shell call) rather than filling a placeholder you mean to fix later. Same for every PR number, sha and label a comment asserts — resolve, then post.
- **When the outcome your ceiling names is mechanically unavailable, stop short and say so — never substitute a riskier action to close the gap.** A routine told to land work through an auto-merging PR cannot when the repository has auto-merge disabled and its checks will not conclude. The gap looks one command wide, and improvising a merge to close it costs more than the unlanded change does. Where a shared delivery procedure exists (Claudinite's `engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`), the merges it licenses — like the direct merge on a base branch that requires nothing, where the arm is rejected "clean status" by design — are the sanctioned path, not a workaround; anything outside them stays unlanded. An open PR plus a plain statement of what could not be armed and why is a complete, honest result. Re-try the mechanism on each run rather than assuming either state is permanent, and drop the workaround the moment it succeeds.
- **A change-gated routine must exclude its *own* writes from its triggers, or it feeds itself.** A routine that commits to, files issues in, or emits artifacts into the same repos it monitors will re-fire on its own output unless every trigger filters it out: its own maintenance commits must not count as "the project changed" (match them by bot-author / `[skip ci]` / a subject convention and exclude — and keep that matcher current with the wording the routine actually writes, or a near-miss silently reads as real work); its own standing-tracker/issue updates must not count as activity (a tracker rewritten every run always sits inside a fixed lookback window, so it re-triggers forever); its own generated plan/report artifact must not count as a repo change. The tell is a routine that fires every cycle on a fleet that is actually quiet. Treat "the routine's inputs never include the routine's outputs" as an invariant when wiring any change-detection signal.
- When an unattended routine takes an **irreversible or outward-facing action** (closing an issue, deleting a branch, sending a message), the spec must **define the trigger condition concretely and default to the safe path** — not just name the action. A bare "close if done" invites a wrong close on a superficial match; "close *only* when the ask is verifiably true of the target's current state — else comment" cannot. State what counts as the condition and where to verify it, and make the reversible option (leave it, comment, escalate) the default whenever the check is inconclusive.
- A `[Merge Without Review]` security warning on a task's own unattended merge is expected, not a finding to escalate — adjudicate it in one step. When a task's declared delivery policy is auto-merge and its target's checks require no human approval (or the arm is rejected `clean status` and a direct merge is the sanctioned path), the harness still flags the completion with a security warning because no human approval appears in the transcript — that is the harness reporting the *shape* of the action, not evaluating whether it was licensed. Confirm the task's declared delivery policy and its outcome ceiling permit the merge, then converge normally; escalating every occurrence to human review would wedge a routine that is designed to merge unattended.
- A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated, so the parent's own end-of-session checks can misread the subagent's activity as its own. Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real.

## Structuring a routine as prose + scripts

Give a recurring routine its own folder — `dev/routines/<routine-name>/` — holding **`routine.md`** (the standard entry point: the spec the agent reads) beside the deterministic scripts it invokes by path, conventionally `preconditions.sh` and `postconditions.sh` (`bash dev/routines/<name>/preconditions.sh`). This shapes the "hard-code the deterministic parts" boundary above into concrete files, governed by four rules:

- **Bracket the agent's judgment between the two scripts, asymmetrically.** `preconditions.sh` is a cheap eligibility gate — on failure the run **skips**, a clean no-op; size it to the cost of a wasted run (when a no-op is cheap and self-correcting, keep the gate broad and err toward running). `postconditions.sh` validates the output — on failure the run is **terminal: mark it failed, never retry**, because a failed postcondition means the lean spec let the agent produce something invalid; surface it for a human to add guiding prose instead of looping.
- **State in `routine.md` every expectation a script enforces.** A validator (scope diff, metric floor, value check) the prose never taught trips the agent on a bar it was never told; a check should only *confirm* an expectation the agent already held, so map each stated rule to the check that guards it. (Complements the write-surface diff-check above: the diff guarantees the bound, the prose has to teach it.)
- **Extract a script only when it takes a whole deterministic decision off the agent.** Wrapping a still-reasoned step, or a lone command beside an un-scriptable one (a `git push` next to an MCP-only PR-open), is indirection — fold it back into the prose. A helper earns its place by consolidating determinism, not by existing.
- **Keep the job — the feedback loop and judgment criteria — in `routine.md`, never only in a script's comments** (scripts are run, not read). description: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.

# Agent architecture principles

Portable rules for *how to structure an unattended (automation-invoked) agent* — the judgment-boundary and write-surface guarantees that keep a workflow-driven agent bounded and reliable, independent of any one project.

- An agent invoked **unattended** by automation (a CI workflow, not interactive Claude Code) should be left only the part of the task that genuinely needs its judgment; hard-code every deterministic part — the setup before *and* the wrap-up after — in the workflow around it. A step described in prose is one the agent can skip, reorder, or improvise; a step the workflow runs in code can't be fumbled, and the shorter prompt keeps the agent on the one thing only it can do. - When a routine needs a capability its own runtime lacks — a credential spanning more repos than the session's allowlist, an execution surface the sandbox can't reach — wrap that part as a **dispatch-only executor** (e.g. a `workflow_dispatch`-only GitHub Actions workflow holding the privileged token) that the routine triggers and awaits. The executor carries **no schedule of its own**: give it a cron and it silently becomes a second orchestrator with a competing trigger. State only the executor's *contract* in the routine's prose (what it computes, what the agent may rely on) — its internal rules live in its code, unlike validators of the agent's *own* output, which the prose must still teach (see the routine-folder rules below).

Keep it to terse imperative bullets stating outcomes, bounds, and judgment criteria; a delegated step gets its contract only, procedure another doc owns gets a pointer (never a restatement), and a why-clause earns its place only where the rule is surprising. Symptoms you've absorbed what belongs elsewhere: the spec re-explains a companion script's logic or a sibling doc's steps, or has grown to several times its sibling routines (the house norm is ~40–90 lines).

Pre-create the exact file(s) it may edit, tell it to touch nothing else (no new files, no edits to shared code it might be tempted to "improve"), and after it stops, verify the diff in the workflow — reverting anything outside the allowed set rather than trusting the prompt. Prose is a request; the post-hoc diff check is the guarantee, so a misbehaving agent's blast radius is bounded no matter how it strays. Anything the agent would otherwise reach into belongs inlined in its own file (as a source's local helper), not edited in place.
- In a multi-stage unattended pipeline, converge **every** failure exit — including an infrastructure failure in a pre-agent setup stage (a fetch, an auth step, scaffolding) — to the same human-triage state as an agent-detected failure. A setup-phase failure that reports itself but leaves the original trigger untouched (e.g. a label still set) makes the item look unprocessed rather than blocked, silently defeating the escalation path. Treat every failure mode as equivalent from the triage perspective.
- An unattended agent must **never invoke a tool that surfaces a blocking approval it cannot answer** — there is no human present to click "Allow," so the run stalls indefinitely on step one. The multi-agent-orchestration **Workflow tool is the classic trap**: it mandates an interactive opt-in on *every* run (the prompt only disappears under bypass-permissions / headless modes you cannot rely on the scheduler being in), so a routine that fans out through it hangs before doing any work. Fan out with **plain subagent dispatch** (the Agent/Task tool) instead — it carries no such gate and the orchestrator honors any phase barriers itself — and reserve the Workflow tool for interactive sessions where a human can consent. The general rule: an unattended agent's whole tool path must be answer-free.
- **Dispatch a subagent under worktree isolation whenever it may commit.** Without it the child works in the parent's checkout and leaves it wherever it finished — on the child's branch — so the parent's branch-scoped end-of-session checks judge the *child's* commits against the *parent's* transcript and file findings the parent cannot act on. Re-try the mechanism on each run rather than assuming either state is permanent, and drop the workaround the moment it succeeds.

## An automated job needs a unique branch per run

An automated or scheduled job that derives its branch name from a non-unique key (e.g. the date) collides with itself on a repeat run for that key — `git checkout -b` fails when the branch already exists, and a push to the diverged remote branch is rejected non-fast-forward (so the run can't even open its PR). Give every run its own branch: append a per-run-unique suffix (`$RANDOM` / a short token) to the readable prefix.

## An unattended workflow must escalate its own failure to a human-visible state

A workflow with no human watching the run — scheduled, triggered by a push/merge, or a fire-and-forget manual dispatch, with no other path that reaches a person — must converge a failure to something a human will see (e.g. open a `workflow-failure` issue for it) rather than merely exiting red in the Actions list, where nobody looks. Skip this only when the failure is already loud: a `pull_request`/push CI run that blocks merge with a red required check the author is watching, or a workflow that already flags the triggering issue itself on failure. The canon's [report-failure](../../../../.github/actions/report-failure/action.yml) action does exactly this — a **fresh** issue per failure, with earlier open failure issues for the same workflow closed as duplicates of the newest — so the current failure is always the single open bug to triage; a standing per-workflow issue appended to on each failure is an equally valid shape, the invariant is only that the red run reaches a person.

When the escalation is itself a separate reusable workflow invoked via `workflow_call`, permissions don't propagate implicitly through the chain: the job that calls it needs the permission explicitly granted (e.g. `issues: write`), and if that reusable workflow in turn calls another one, the middle workflow must forward the same grant to its own call — a caller two levels up granting it once is not enough.

## A CI job that inspects commit shape must check out the PR head, not the merge ref

On `pull_request`, `actions/checkout` checks out the synthetic `refs/pull/N/merge` commit by default — an ephemeral merge of the PR head into the base — so `HEAD` is itself a merge commit, not the branch tip. Any job that reasons about commit *shape* or history (merge commits, commit count, `--first-parent`, commit messages) reads that synthetic merge and misfires: a "no merge commits" check false-positives even on a linear branch, since `HEAD` is a merge. Check out the head SHA (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}`) so CI evaluates the same branch tip a local run does.

## To read a PR's CI result, look at its check runs — `get_status` misses Actions

GitHub **Actions** reports results as **check runs**, not the legacy **commit statuses**, so `pull_request_read` `method: get_status` returns `state: pending`, `total_count: 0` for a PR whose Actions CI has already **passed** — reading falsely as "no CI / not started," which can skip a real gate or trigger an endless wait. Gate on CI by reading the **check runs for the PR head SHA** (`get_check_run`, or the workflow run for that SHA) instead. Target the head SHA directly rather than `actions_list`-ing the repo's runs — that returns every run, its output is huge, and a specific check-run/SHA query is both correct and cheap.

## To confirm a non-PR run (push / dispatch), read its job logs — it has no PR check runs

A `push` or `workflow_dispatch` run isn't attached to a PR, so the PR-scoped check-run query above doesn't apply to it. Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. `get_job_logs` needs more than a bare `run_id`: it rejects with "job_id is required when failed_only is false" unless you pass `failed_only: true` or fetch a `job_id` first (`list_workflow_jobs`), and it 404s for a job still `in_progress` — wait for the job to finish. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.

## A green run is not evidence its job ran — read the job's own conclusion

A workflow that gates a later job (an `if:` on changed paths, a mode flag, a preceding job's output) concludes **success** with that job **skipped** — so "the release workflow is green" is not evidence the publish step ever executed, and most green runs may never have reached it. Read the conclusion of the **job that does the thing**, never the run's. The corollary for closing an issue: the only closing evidence is a run that actually reached that job and went green, or the external system showing the effect. Fixing a repo-side defect that merely co-occurred with the failure verifies nothing, and a failure caused by state in an external service has no fix in the repo at all.

## To confirm a non-PR run (push / dispatch), read its job logs — it has no PR check runs

A `push` or `workflow_dispatch` run isn't attached to a PR, so the PR-scoped check-run query above doesn't apply to it. Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. `get_job_logs` needs more than a bare `run_id`: it rejects with "job_id is required when failed_only is false" unless you pass `failed_only: true` or fetch a `job_id` first (`list_workflow_jobs`), and it 404s for a job still `in_progress` — wait for the job to finish. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.

## A green run is not evidence its job ran — read the job's own conclusion

A workflow that gates a later job (an `if:` on changed paths, a mode flag, a preceding job's output) concludes **success** with that job **skipped** — so "the release workflow is green" is not evidence the publish step ever executed, and most green runs may never have reached it. Read the conclusion of the **job that does the thing**, never the run's. The corollary for closing an issue: the only closing evidence is a run that actually reached that job and went green, or the external system showing the effect. Fixing a repo-side defect that merely co-occurred with the failure verifies nothing, and a failure caused by state in an external service has no fix in the repo at all.

# git-github — the git/GitHub domain pack

The git/GitHub side of the task lifecycle, bundled as skills: the advanced procedures
([git-github-advanced](skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md) — commit layering, squash-merge
recovery, CI-trigger rules, merge-relocation traps) and the owner's merge command
([merge-to-main](skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md) — "LGTM").

No prose and no checks of its own — the lifecycle checks (`task-lifecycle`,
`squash-merge-history`) stay in `basics`. Every repo gets this pack through `basics`'s
`requires` closure (materialized into declarations at `--init` and the baselining backfill),
never by direct seeding.
=====HEADLESS-BROWSER=====
# headless-browser pack

Active when the repo references a browser-automation driver in JS/TS source — a `playwright` /
`playwright-core` / `puppeteer` / `puppeteer-core` module specifier, or a `.launch(` call site.
Scanning source rather than a dependency manifest is deliberate: a repo can drive a browser its
environment image already installs, with no dependency entry anywhere to find.

Prose only. Every rule is a runtime browser behaviour or a judgment about a harness's shape,
neither of which has a repo-state signature a check could read without asserting that a
particular call still exists — the shape the corpus rejects outright.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resolve binary, never download | high | correctness | prose: 123 words |
| Reinstalling the driver repeats the download danger | high | correctness | prose: 77 words |
| Pin the build for pixels | high | correctness | prose: 87 words |
| Zero-diff costs whole recipe | medium | correctness | prose: 95 words |
| Fake origin, abort by default | high | correctness | prose: 80 words |
| `https` origin for geolocation | medium | correctness | prose: 48 words |
| Route vendored assets host-agnostically | medium | correctness | prose: 75 words |
| Context knobs vs page knobs | medium | correctness | prose: 67 words |
| Window-size flag isn't a viewport | high | correctness | prose: 132 words |
| Fakes as init scripts | high | correctness | prose: 42 words |
| CSS freeze misses `element.animate` | high | correctness | prose: 45 words |
| Two clock modes | medium | correctness | prose: 55 words |
| Font jail, not just webfonts | high | correctness | prose: 111 words |
| Reproducible rasterisation flags | high | correctness | prose: 60 words |
| Wait on the page's signal | high | correctness | prose: 66 words |
| Clip, don't screenshot the element | medium | correctness | prose: 65 words |
| Bounding boxes go stale | medium | correctness | prose: 59 words |
| Whole-pixel clips | medium | correctness | prose: 57 words |
| Strip scripts needing the runtime | medium | correctness | prose: 53 words |
| One browser, many contexts | medium | performance | prose: 51 words |

## Boundary

The [writing-tests](../basics/skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md) skill owns which engine a UI golden
should use, the tolerance a browser golden may carry, self-skipping where no browser is present,
and the re-baselining approval gate — this pack restates none of it, and its "zero-diff costs the
whole recipe" rule is written to complement that guidance rather than contradict it.
[github-actions](../github-actions/) owns wiring the run into a workflow.

Provenance: distilled from three fleet members that drive a browser from code, independently and
for different reasons. `missingbulb/EdFringeNow` — a pinned-Chromium visual-requirements harness:
fake-origin routing, the font jail, rasterisation flags, clip and bounding-box mechanics.
`missingbulb/CrosswordChat` — browser rasterisation for both goldens and generated build
artifacts: environment binary resolution, stripping runtime-dependent scripts.
`missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite` — an interactive responsive check: the window-size-is-not-a-
viewport footgun and the virtual-time budget. The first two solved the cross-machine rendering
problem two different ways, which is what the pinning rules carry.
`missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator` holds a vestigial fourth instance in a retired prototype.

input.old_string: - A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated, so the parent's own end-of-session checks can misread the subagent's activity as its own. Without `isolation: "worktree"`, a background agent runs in the *same* checkout as the session that spawned it, so while it's running: its uncommitted WIP can look like the parent's own dirty diff to a git-status-based finding, and if it switches branches (e.g. checking out another branch to inspect or fix it), a check that reads the current branch now reads *its* branch, not the parent's. Before diagnosing such a finding as your own — one naming "the branch" or "the commit", or unreferenced/uncommitted changes — check whether a background agent is still running; if a mid-dispatch finding names a branch other than the one you were assigned, switch back to your own branch to clear it rather than treating the finding as real.

lines: - When an unattended routine takes an **irreversible or outward-facing action** (closing an issue, deleting a branch, sending a message), the spec must **define the trigger condition concretely and default to the safe path** — not just name the action. A bare "close if done" invites a wrong close on a superficial match; "close *only* when the ask is verifiably true of the target's current state — else comment" cannot. State what counts as the condition and where to verify it, and make the reversible option (leave it, comment, escalate) the default whenever the check is inconclusive.

- A `[Merge Without Review]` security warning on a task's own unattended merge is expected, not a finding to escalate — adjudicate it in one step. When a task's declared delivery policy is auto-merge and its target's checks require no human approval (or the arm is rejected `clean status` and a direct merge is the sanctioned path), the harness still flags the completion with a security warning because no human approval appears in the transcript — that is the harness reporting the *shape* of the action, not evaluating whether it was licensed. Confirm the task's declared delivery policy and its outcome ceiling permit the merge, then converge normally; escalating every occurrence to human review would wedge a routine that is designed to merge unattended.

- A background subagent dispatch shares the parent's working directory unless isolated, so the parent's own end-of-session checks can misread the subagent's activity as its own. # Headless browser

Driving a real browser from your own process — a page loaded, faked, driven and captured by code
rather than by a user. True whether the output is a golden image, a build artifact, or an
assertion about behaviour, and whether the driver is Playwright or Puppeteer.

Two neighbours own ground this pack deliberately does not restate: **which** engine a UI golden
should be rendered with, what tolerance it may carry, and the approval gate before re-baselining
one belong to the [writing-tests](../basics/skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md) skill; wiring the run
into a workflow belongs to [github-actions](../github-actions/). This pack is the browser itself.

## Getting a browser

- **Resolve the binary out of the environment; never let the driver download one.** A container
  or runner image that already ships a browser is the normal case, and the driver's own registry
  download is slow, often blocked, and pins a build you did not choose. Look for an explicit
  override variable first, then the image's browser root, then fall through to the driver's own
  resolution — and prefer the driver's `-core` package, which bundles no browser at all. The
  image's build number need not match the driver's own pin for the browser to launch. Never
  hardcode the version-stamped path you found by looking: it moves with the next image, and the
  failure lands on whoever rebuilds rather than on whoever wrote it.

- **A fresh install of the driver package is the same danger from upstream.** Reinstalling the
  package to fix an import error just as easily resolves to a newer release than the one paired
  with the environment's pinned browser — it then hunts for a browser build the image was never
  given and fails asking for a network install the sandbox cannot make. Resolve the
  already-installed package by its global path instead of adding a second copy.

- **A committed pixel golden is only comparable under the exact build that rendered it.** Two
  browsers a version apart rasterise text and shadows differently, so a comparison across them
  measures the renderer, not the product. Where the output is compared pixel by pixel, read the
  installed driver version at launch and **refuse to run** on any other, naming the pinned one in
  the error; where it is not — a build artifact, a behavioural assertion — let the build float
  and spend nothing on pinning it.

- **Pinning is what buys a zero-diff browser golden — budget for the whole recipe or accept a
  tolerance.** A browser screenshot is not bit-stable across machines by default, which is why
  the general advice is a small tolerance. It *can* be made bit-stable, and the price is this
  pack's next two sections in full: the pinned build, a font jail, and the rasterisation flags.
  Take all of it or take the tolerance; a half-applied recipe gives a zero-diff gate that fails
  on someone else's machine for reasons no one can read off the diff.

## The page's world is an input — replace all of it

- **Serve the page from a fake origin you fulfil from disk, and abort anything you did not
  name.** Intercepting at the browser needs no server process, no port and no free-port race,
  and it reaches *every* request the page makes rather than the ones an application-level mock
  happens to know about. Make the default arm an abort: a new external dependency then breaks
  the run loudly instead of quietly adding real network to a run meant to be hermetic.

- **Use an `https` fake origin.** Geolocation and several other capabilities exist only on a
  secure origin, and a page served over `http` silently takes the denied path instead. Routes
  are fulfilled before any connection is attempted, so no certificate is involved and nothing
  has to be trusted.

- **Route a vendored third-party asset host-agnostically.** A stylesheet you serve in place of a
  CDN copy still resolves *its own* relative URLs against the host it was served from, so the
  font or image files it references arrive addressed to that CDN. Match those follow-up requests
  on the path alone, on any host, or the sheet loads and every asset it names 404s — which
  renders as a silent fallback rather than an error.

- **Know which knobs are fixed at context creation and which are per page.** Locale, timezone,
  viewport, device scale factor, geolocation and permissions belong to the browser *context* and
  cannot be changed once it exists — so proving that a product reads a fixed zone rather than
  the device's takes **two** contexts, not one page reconfigured twice. The clock, seeded
  randomness and injected scripts are per page.

- **A command-line window-size flag is not a viewport — a narrow one does not test the narrow
  layout.** Ask a browser's *CLI* for a phone-sized window and it renders the page at a clamped
  width and crops the overflow, without applying the media queries the width should have
  triggered. The output looks exactly like a horizontal-overflow bug in every section of a page
  that has none, and the instinct is to go hunting through the CSS for the offender. Only a
  context or page created with an explicit viewport puts the page in that layout. Reserve the
  CLI screenshot for the width the window happens to be, and give it a virtual-time budget that
  outlasts the page's entrance animations, or sections capture mid-transition and read as broken
  when they are fine.

- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.

- **Freezing CSS animation does not freeze the Web Animations API.** Zeroing
  `animation-duration` and `transition-duration` stops declarative animation and nothing else;
  anything driven through `element.animate` keeps running, and a capture races it. Stub the
  method so every such animation resolves on its end state immediately.

- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
  has no timers to advance.

## Fonts decide the layout, and the machine decides the fonts

- **Vendoring the web fonts is half the job — every glyph they lack is drawn from the machine.**
  An emoji, an arrow, a currency sign, a non-Latin title: each falls back to whatever the host
  has installed, so the rendering quietly becomes a record of that machine's font set. The
  failure is brutal and unobvious — one string measures wider on a runner than on a workstation,
  wraps, and every card below it moves down a line. Launch the browser with its own
  font-configuration world whose only font directory is one you vendored, with the generic
  families aliased into it, so nothing installed on the host can reach the page.

- **Ask the browser for reproducible rasterisation.** Disable hinting and subpixel text, force
  an sRGB colour profile, hide scrollbars, and disable GPU rasterisation. Shadows and blurs need
  two more: partial raster reuses tiles whose seams land inside a blur, and runtime-optimised
  drawing routines differ by CPU — both make the *same* page render differently run to run on
  one machine.

## Capturing

- **Wait on something the page itself produces, never on the network going quiet.** A selector
  that only exists once data rendered, or text that only appears once an async read returned, is
  a real signal; "no requests for a moment" is a guess that is wrong in both directions. Await
  font readiness too — text laid out before the fonts land is a different image.

- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
  deliberately before measuring anything.

- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.

- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
  is an error, not a crop.

- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
  meant to show yourself.

- **Launch once and reuse the browser across captures.** Process startup dominates the cost of a
  capture, so a fresh browser per shot turns a fast run into a slow one for nothing; take a new
  context or page per capture instead, and close it, so no state leaks between them.

# headless-browser pack
